title: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy selectively affecting Broca's and Wernicke's areas in an immunocompetent patient: A case report
case_prompt:
A 74-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, prior stroke, and possible Sjögren’s-related vasculitis presented with six weeks of gradually worsening receptive and expressive aphasia. Initial laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and urinalysis. A noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. A brain MRI and MRA performed 10 days before presentation demonstrated new patchy FLAIR hyperintensities in the left inferior frontal gyrus and left temporoparietal white matter, sparing gray matter, concerning for a vasculitis flare or subacute ischemia. The patient was admitted for further evaluation. 

A lumbar puncture revealed normal cell counts and differential but a positive JCV PCR at 201 copies/mL. The cerebrospinal fluid autoimmune encephalopathy antibody panel was negative. Two weeks later, a repeat lumbar puncture again showed JCV PCR positivity (73 copies/mL) but was negative for cytomegalovirus, varicella-zoster virus, herpes-simplex virus, and human immunodeficiency virus. One-month follow-up MRI showed minimal progression of the white-matter lesions. A CT angiogram of the head and neck showed no evidence of vasculitis. 

Autoimmune serologic testing revealed a positive anti-SSa/anti-Ro antibody but negative antinuclear, rheumatoid factor, cyclic citrullinated peptide, and antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies. C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, thyroid-stimulating hormone, C3, and C4 levels were within normal limits. Serum protein electrophoresis showed mildly decreased total protein and albumin but was otherwise normal. None of the subsequent laboratory tests showed any indicator of ongoing immunosuppression.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Vasculitis was initially considered due to MRI findings suggesting inflammatory disease — “new patchy hyperintense FLAIR signal … concerning at the time for a vasculitis flare or subacute ischemia.”  
2. Subacute ischemia was also on the differential because the white-matter hyperintensities could represent evolving infarcts — “new patchy hyperintense FLAIR signal … concerning at the time for a vasculitis flare or subacute ischemia.”  
3. Autoimmune encephalopathy was considered but excluded after negative antibody testing — “The cerebrospinal fluid autoimmune encephalopathy antibody panel was negative.”  
4. Cytomegalovirus infection was ruled out by cerebrospinal fluid PCR — “negative for cytomegalovirus…”  
5. Varicella-zoster virus infection was ruled out by cerebrospinal fluid PCR — “negative for … varicella-zoster virus…”  
6. Herpes-simplex virus infection was ruled out by cerebrospinal fluid PCR — “negative for … herpes-simplex virus…”  
7. HIV infection was excluded by negative cerebrospinal fluid testing — “negative for … human immunodeficiency virus.”  
8. Occult immunosuppression from conditions such as hepatic cirrhosis or renal failure was considered unlikely given the patient’s lack of relevant comorbidities — “Our patient did not have any comorbid conditions that would be concerning for occult immunosuppression.”
